blogs.title: Intrinsic or 404(b)? The Eighth Circuit’s Elastic Approach to Prior Firearm Possession
blogs.description: The panel leans on United States v. Battle to uphold testimony that witnesses had seen the defendant with the same sawed-off rifle before the charged incident, treating it as “intrinsic” to the felon-in-possession charge rather than Rule 404(b) propensity evidence. This post examines how the Eighth Circuit’s intrinsic-evidence doctrine continues to sweep in prior-acts proof when it helps establish identity, ownership, or continuity of possession, and assesses the risks of propensity creep. We’ll compare the Eighth Circuit’s treatment to other circuits’ narrowing of “intrinsic” evidence post-404(b) amendments, and consider trial practice implications for framing and limiting such testimony.

blogs.title: ‘Context’ Testimony, Limiting Instructions, and the Confrontation Clause: A Quiet Win for Prosecutors
blogs.description: Cutbank’s bid for a preemptive limiting instruction to cabin officers’ recounting of the victim’s statements went nowhere. The court emphasizes that admitting non-hearsay background to explain police conduct, coupled with the declarant’s in-court testimony, satisfies both hearsay limits and the Confrontation Clause. This post unpacks the Eighth Circuit’s deference on the timing of limiting instructions, the line between context and hearsay, and how Charboneau resolves confrontation concerns when the declarant testifies. We also touch on the court’s harmless-error backstop and what defense counsel can do to preserve and sharpen these issues.

blogs.title: Stacking Enhancements in an ACCA Case: §2K2.1(b)(6)(B), §4B1.4, and the Presumption of Reasonableness
blogs.description: At sentencing, the district court applied §2K2.1(b)(6)(B)’s four-level enhancement for possessing the gun in connection with another felony, even though ACCA already drove a severe penalty and §4B1.4 would have yielded a slightly lower offense level. The panel affirms, stressing accurate Guidelines calculation, the directive to apply the greater offense level, and a strong within-Guidelines presumption of reasonableness. This post analyzes double-counting concerns, the role of uncharged conduct via Application Note 14(C), and the Eighth Circuit’s approach to §3553(a) variance arguments in violent firearm cases. We also consider strategic takeaways for contesting nexus findings and framing substantive reasonableness arguments post-Gall.

blogs.title: Impeachment by Police Reports and Appellate Discipline: Authentication Matters
blogs.description: Defense efforts to read from a police report during impeachment were curtailed for lack of foundation, a ruling the panel endorses under Cumbie’s authentication requirement for extrinsic impeachment evidence. Notably, the court also chides the government for “unnecessarily” expanding the issues on appeal—an appellate-practice warning. This post offers practical guidance on using prior inconsistent statements embedded in third-party reports, how to lay the groundwork for admission, and why over-briefing on appeal can irk a panel. We also briefly survey the court’s 403 tolerance for emotionally charged but context-linked statements (e.g., the victim’s reference to her sister’s shooting) and how to mitigate potential prejudice.
